findings.headline: Authorized borrowing of £580m but forecast only £330m—43% gap
findings.detail: The council's authorized limit for external debt borrowing is set at £580m, yet the 2026/27 forecast is £330m, against a budgeted £497m for external debt loans. This consistent pattern across debt categories suggests either conservative forecasting or constraints on executing planned capital schemes.
findings.matters: Large gaps between authorized and forecast borrowing raise questions about whether capital plans are at risk or whether assumptions have shifted. A lender would need to understand why actual deployment falls so far short of authorization.
findings.figures: Authorized £580m, Forecast £330m, Budgeted loans £497m
findings.quote: External Debt – Authorised Limit for borrowing 580 330

findings.headline: Long-term investment forecast cut 88% from budget: £245m to £30m
findings.detail: The upper limit for principal sums to be invested for longer than a year is forecast at £30m, down sharply from the budgeted £245.0m. This 88% reduction suggests either significantly constrained cash deployment or major deferrals of planned investment.
findings.matters: A dramatic cut in planned investment signifies either tighter liquidity or deferred capital schemes. Either would concern a lender assessing the council's cash flow and capital programme delivery.
findings.figures: Budget £245.0m, Forecast £30m
findings.quote: Upper limit for total principal sums invested for longer than a year 245.0 30

findings.headline: LOBO loans with uncertain call dates create refinancing risk the council cannot quantify with standard limits
findings.detail: The council holds LOBO loans (Lender Option Borrower Option) where the lender can force early repayment at specified points. This creates uncertainty that prevents using the standard practice of limiting debt maturity to 15% per year. Instead, the council manages exposure via a stress-test graph, acknowledging 'the actual pattern of repayment, although uncertain, will not be of this magnitude.'
findings.matters: LOBO calls create refinancing risk that is not fully predictable; if called, the council must refinance at prevailing market rates regardless of the interest rate environment.
findings.figures: No breakdown given for LOBO holdings; limits are shown in graph at Appendix 1
findings.quote: LOBO loans with uncertain call dates and the use of internal cash, specific indicators have not been set. Instead, the County Council will manage its exposures within the limits shown in the graph at Appendix 1.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Report for the Year Ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Lender exercised call option on £15 million LOBO, forcing refinancing at higher rates
findings.detail: The council was forced to repay a £15 million LOBO early when the lender exercised call options due to rising interest rates. This demonstrates the refinancing risk embedded in LOBO structures where the lender controls timing.
findings.matters: Shows the council carries LOBOs with embedded lender options that could force refinancing at adverse rates when markets move against the council
findings.figures: £15.000 million LOBO repaid early
findings.quote: the County Council repaid a £15.000 million LOBO loan early due to the lender exercising their call options and increasing the interest rate.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Report for the Year Ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Gilt yields spiked sharply in March 2026 due to Middle East conflict and remain elevated
findings.detail: PWLB rates rose significantly in March 2026 following geopolitical events and have remained high. Treasury advisers forecast Bank Rate will stay at 3.75% through 2026/27, but markets expect rates may hold or increase to combat inflation.
findings.matters: The council's strategy of using internal cash to avoid borrowing depends on access to reasonable future rates; persistent higher rates would increase costs for any future borrowing
findings.figures: Bank Rate reduced to 3.75% in December 2025 and held at that level; PWLB rates spiked in March 2026
findings.quote: Gilt yields rose significantly in March 2026 at the start of the Middle East conflict and have remained elevated since.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Report for the Year Ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Lending to other local authorities has quintupled to £152 million in one year
findings.detail: The council increased short-term investments in other local authorities from £30 million to £152 million in 2025/26, driven by competitive interest rates. This now represents one-third of total investments concentrated across 25 different councils.
findings.matters: Shows the council has excess liquidity but also significant concentration risk in other councils that may face their own financial pressures
findings.figures: £30 million (31 March 2025) to £152 million (31 March 2026)
findings.quote: Investment in LAs has increased during 2025/26 due to the competitive interest rates on offer for short term investments in this category.

findings.headline: Children's Services required significant investment and restructuring following Ofsted 'requires improvement' judgment; continuing demand pressures flagged
findings.detail: Following November 2023 Ofsted inspection, council invested significantly in new leadership and wholesale restructure plus new children's social care IT system. June 2026 inspection praised improvements but identified need to focus on staff capacity in context of continually increasing demand and pace of change.
findings.matters: Children's Services is a major budget area; significant investment requirement signals prior service failure and ongoing spending pressures; increasing demand suggests costs may not stabilise.
findings.figures: New DCS appointed July 2024; focused visit November 2025; joint targeted area inspection June 2026
findings.quote: A number of recommendations were made including a need to focus on the capacity of staff to deliver quality practice in the context of continually increasing demand.

findings.headline: Major financial management system replacement required during Local Government Reorganisation transformation
findings.detail: The council is implementing a replacement financial management system alongside new Adults and Children's case management systems during major organisational change. The council must maintain effective control of core operations whilst undertaking this significant transformation.
findings.matters: System replacement during major organisational restructuring creates implementation risk; system failures could impair the council's ability to prepare timely and accurate financial statements and manage budgets effectively.
findings.figures: LGR notification anticipated Summer 2026; multiple new systems implementation required
findings.quote: This includes the implementation of a replacement financial management system and Adults and Children's case management system.

findings.headline: Payment control weaknesses identified in purchase cards, SEND Direct Payments, and Out of Hours Highways Service
findings.detail: Counter-fraud exercises identified weaknesses in payment controls across these specific areas. Several limited assurance opinions were awarded and internal audit will continue supporting these areas in 2026/27 to establish robust control environments.
findings.matters: Payment control weaknesses create fraud and error risk; SEND Direct Payments represents a growing area of spend to vulnerable service users.
findings.figures: Multiple high-level recommendations issued; multiple limited assurance opinions in payment control reviews
findings.quote: The proactive counter-fraud exercises (CCM work) have continued to identify weaknesses in payment controls, especially regarding purchase cards, SEND Direct Payments and Out of Hours Highways Service. Several limited assurance report opinions have been awarded in this area as a result.

findings.headline: Schools compliance programme revealed persistent control weaknesses affecting 13 of 18 schools audited
findings.detail: Of 18 schools audited, 13 received limited assurance ratings due to non-compliance with regulations and internal control lapses including within school payroll processes. Although the number receiving positive assurance has increased compared to 2024/25, schools compliance remains flagged as requiring continued audit attention.
findings.matters: Schools represent significant public funding streams; payroll control lapses and non-compliance create fraud and financial risk, suggesting underlying control environment gaps.
findings.figures: 13 of 18 schools audited (72%) received limited assurance ratings
findings.quote: The Schools' Compliance Programme revealed ongoing issues. Of the 18 schools audited, 13 received limited assurance ratings due to non-compliance with Regulations and internal control lapses including within school payroll processes.

findings.headline: Four consecutive years of disclaimed audit opinions on financial statements (2021/22 to 2024/25)
findings.detail: The council has received disclaimed opinions from both EY (2021/22, 2022/23) and KPMG (2023/24, 2024/25). A disclaimed opinion means the auditor could not obtain sufficient evidence to form an opinion on the financial statements. KPMG noted improvements and progress in coverage and assurances during 2024/25 but still issued a disclaimed opinion.
findings.matters: Disclaimed audit opinions mean financial statements cannot be relied upon; they create uncertainty about the accuracy of the council's reported financial position and its ability to service debt.
findings.figures: Four consecutive financial years with disclaimed opinions: 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25
findings.quote: Given the receipt of disclaimed opinions from EY for the 2021/22 and 2022/23 financial years statements, a further disclaimed opinion was also given for the 2023/24 financial statements by KPMG... A further disclaimed opinion was given for the 2024/25 Financial Statements.

findings.headline: Local government reorganisation to unitary status in April 2028 identified as top risk area for 2025/26
findings.detail: The council is heading towards unitary status in April 2028, and this structural reorganisation has been identified as a top risk area for internal audit oversight. Internal Audit is providing support to the council and services as they transition during 2025/26.
findings.matters: Structural reorganisation of local government creates significant operational and financial risk during transition periods; control breakdowns, duplicate functions, service disruptions, and integration failures commonly occur during such reshaping.

findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation – To provide support to the Council and services in year as it heads towards unitary status in April 2028.

findings.detail: The external auditor raised a performance improvement observation regarding Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP) completion rates, recommending continued transparency and improvement to meet targets. The auditor also noted a performance improvement observation relating to governance and the SEND position more broadly.
findings.matters: SEND and EHCP is a nationally significant financial pressure area for councils; completion rate issues indicate service backlogs that could drive future expenditure pressures and indicate the council is unable to meet statutory timescales.

findings.headline: Counter-fraud exercises identified weaknesses in purchase card and SEND Direct Payment controls
findings.detail: Proactive counter-fraud work identified ongoing weaknesses in payment controls, particularly for purchase cards and SEND Direct Payments. Although overall financial losses from fraud remained low in 2024/25, concerns persist in compliance reviews. Internal Audit has included further work in these areas within the 2026/27 plan.
findings.matters: Payment control weaknesses are a fundamental financial control failure, and SEND Direct Payments represent high-risk financial flows; weaknesses in both areas indicate that preventive controls are not effective.
findings.figures: Limited assurance opinions in system reviews decreased from nine in 2023/24 to five in 2024/25
findings.quote: The proactive counter-fraud exercises continued to identify weaknesses in payment controls, especially regarding purchase cards and SEND Direct Payments.

findings.detail: The Schools' Compliance Programme revealed that 19 out of 21 schools audited received limited assurance ratings due to non-compliance with regulations and internal control lapses. These lapses included failures within school payroll processes. Internal Audit is now planning to use AI in 2025/26 to support schools in strengthening controls.
findings.matters: Schools represent a significant operational and financial component of local authorities; payroll control failures are fundamental governance weaknesses, and widespread non-compliance across 90% of sampled schools indicates a material control environment issue.
findings.figures: 19 of 21 schools
findings.quote: Of the 21 schools audited, 19 received limited assurance ratings due to non-compliance with Regulations and internal control lapses including within school payroll processes.

findings.paper_title: Annual Report of the Audit & Standards Committee - 2025- 2026
findings.headline: External auditor issued a disclaimed opinion on 2024/25 accounts, with audit completion delayed to 28 February 2026
findings.detail: The audit of the Statement of Accounts for 2024/25 was not completed until 28 February 2026 and was awarded a disclaimed opinion. This position was carried forward from the previous year due to incomplete work by the statutory deadline. The pension fund accounts would have received a clean opinion if separate, but the authority's accounts were disclaimed due to incomplete audit work.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means the external auditor cannot provide assurance on the accuracy and completeness of the financial statements, which is a fundamental concern for any lender assessing financial reliability.
findings.figures: 28 February 2026
findings.quote: the audit was completed by 28 February 2026, with a disclaimed opinion being awarded

findings.headline: Invoice payment delays and aged debt in SEND Managed Accounts indicate cash flow or process management issues not being resolved
findings.detail: The Direct Payments Managed Accounts audit found that three out of six invoices sampled were not paid within the required 28-day timescale, and flagged high levels of aged debt with managed account providers. The guidance for managing these accounts is outdated and does not clearly define roles and responsibilities. There is no formal process for verifying provider performance or escalating concerns.
findings.matters: Payment delays to care providers can affect service continuity and damage relationships. Aged debt suggests either cash flow stress or poor controls. This is a sign of operational dysfunction that could cascade into service failures.
findings.figures: 3 out of 6 invoices not paid within 28 days; high amount of aged debt with managed account providers
findings.quote: Invoice Payment & Aged Debt: Three out of six invoices had not been paid within the 28 days required. There is a high amount of aged debt with managed account providers that has not been paid.

findings.headline: Fraud and error losses of £57,109 identified with control weaknesses specifically in purchase cards and SEND direct payments requiring continued management action
findings.detail: Internal audit identified £57,109 in confirmed/estimated fraud and error losses across special investigations (£31,947 including one case referred to police), National Fraud Initiative (£2,643), and proactive fraud exercises (£22,519). The audit notes these losses came from "lapses in the application of controls" and specifically flags weakness in purchase card and SEND direct payment controls as areas where proactive testing continues to identify errors. The threshold for material impact is £300,000, so this is below material but shows persistent control weaknesses.
findings.matters: Fraud losses indicate control failures that could indicate systemic issues or cultural problems. The specific identification of recurring payment control weaknesses in SEND and purchase cards suggests management has not yet resolved root causes.
findings.figures: £31,947 internal special investigations (includes case referred to police); £2,643 National Fraud Initiative; £22,519 proactive fraud exercises; £57,109 total; threshold for material impact is £300,000
findings.quote: The proactive counter-fraud exercises (CCM work) have continued to identify weaknesses in payment controls, especially regarding purchase cards, SEND Direct Payments and Out of Hours Highways Service. Several limited assurance report opinions have been awarded in this area as a result

findings.headline: Overall audit opinion declined to Adequate Assurance (not Substantial) because compliance reviews and fraud controls failed the 90% benchmark
findings.detail: Staffordshire's control environment opinion dropped because only 3 of 5 audit categories met the 90% adequacy benchmark. Compliance reviews achieved only 66% adequate-or-above opinions (primarily due to schools failures), and Special Investigations/Fraud scored 80%. The report notes this is driven by ongoing issues in maintained schools, weaknesses in payment controls identified through proactive fraud work, and lapses in SEND Direct Payments.
findings.matters: Adequate (rather than Substantial) Assurance means the council's financial and control frameworks have material weaknesses. This is the threshold at which auditors would flag governance concerns to external stakeholders.
findings.figures: Key Risk Areas 100% pass; Main Financial Systems 100% pass; Other System Audits 94% pass; Compliance Reviews 66% fail; Special Investigations 80% fail. Requires 5 of 5 for Substantial, achieved only 3 of 5
findings.quote: Based on the above, an 'Adequate Assurance' opinion has been given on the overall adequacy and effectiveness of the organisation's governance, risk, and control framework, i.e., the control environment in 2025/26.

findings.headline: Schools compliance audit shows 72% of audited schools failed assurance, with widespread governance and payment control failures
findings.detail: Thirteen out of eighteen maintained schools received Limited Assurance opinions in 2025/26. The audit identified failures across financial governance, income banking, payroll, purchase cards, and procurement. Specific issues include: 93% of schools have procurement failures (no purchase orders raised), 79% have purchase card VAT treatment errors, 64% lack segregation of duties on payroll, and 57% have payroll authorisation failures. While the percentage receiving positive assurance improved from 5% in 2024/25 to 28% in 2025/26, the majority remain non-compliant.
findings.matters: Schools manage public funds delegated from the council. Widespread control failures suggest material risk of misuse, fraud, or non-compliance with financial regulations across a significant part of the council's estate.
findings.figures: 13 of 18 schools audited (72%) received Limited Assurance; 93% procurement issues; 79% PCard VAT errors; 64% payroll segregation of duties failures; 57% payroll authorisation failures
findings.quote: For those schools being awarded a limited assurance opinion, issues were found relating to a number of financial administrative areas including school governance; independent oversight of the school fund account; the proper accounting and banking of income; debt recovery including the management of Parentpay debt, compliance with Schools' Procurement Regulations; purchase card use; lettings governance and administration processes

findings.headline: SEND Direct Payments audits awarded Limited Assurance with evidence of unverified expenditure and non-recovery of inappropriate payments
findings.detail: Two separate SEND audits failed assurance: Direct Payments Managed Accounts and SEND Personal Budget & Direct Payments. The Managed Accounts audit flagged that three out of six invoices were not paid within required 28-day timescales and there is high aged debt. The Personal Budget audit found no evidence of expenditure verification and no recorded outcomes for potentially inappropriate payments, with no monies recovered. Review actions agreed in previous audits have not been completed.
findings.matters: Direct payment controls are a known fraud risk, and the failure to verify expenditure or recover improper payments suggests money may be spent without proper authorisation or oversight. This is a core control failure in a high-risk service area.
findings.figures: Three out of six invoices not paid within 28 days; high amount of aged debt; no evidence of expenditure requested for payments
findings.quote: Verification of Expenditure: Evidence of expenditure is not requested to ensure that expenditure is as per the agreed personal budget. Outcomes: There is no recorded outcome for payments which have been highlighted as potentially inappropriate, and no monies returned.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Plan and Strategy Memorandum (2025/26) – Staffordshire County Council
findings.headline: PFI, lease and infrastructure assets audit incomplete due to backstop date timing pressure
findings.detail: The auditor was unable to complete planned audit procedures on PFI, lease, third-party financing liabilities and infrastructure assets in the 2024/25 audit due to the 27 February 2026 backstop deadline. These remain unaudited areas.
findings.matters: Infrastructure, PFI and lease liabilities can be material to a council's financial position. Their non-audit represents a gap in assurance over significant balance sheet items and off-balance-sheet commitments.
findings.figures: Multiple asset categories with incomplete audit procedures deferred to 2025/26
findings.quote: Due to the timing of the audit, there was insufficient time ahead of the backstop date of 27 February 2026 to complete the planned audit procedures

findings.paper_title: External Audit Plan and Strategy Memorandum (2025/26) – Staffordshire County Council
findings.headline: Employee benefit expense audit procedures hampered by delays and poor-quality evidence from services
findings.detail: During the 2024/25 audit, the auditor experienced delays in receiving responses from services and identified that the quality of audit evidence was not sufficient. The council has been asked to ensure evidence is from external or third-party sources where possible.
findings.matters: Poor evidence provision and delays in the audit process suggest either resource constraints or organisational challenges in finance controls, and may indicate wider issues with management's commitment to financial reporting discipline.
findings.figures: Employee benefit expense balance not fully audited in 2024/25
findings.quote: We experienced delays in receiving responses to queries from services and the quality of some audit evidence was not sufficient

findings.paper_title: External Audit Plan and Strategy Memorandum (2025/26) – Staffordshire County Council
findings.headline: Journal entry control deficiency: large volume of non-balancing journals delayed 2024/25 audit
findings.detail: In the 2024/25 audit, the auditor identified a large volume of journals that did not individually balance to zero, requiring management to invest significant time to resolve. This issue delayed audit procedures and meant the auditor could not conclude on the risk of management override of controls.
findings.matters: Journal entry controls are fundamental to preventing and detecting fraud and material error. A deficiency of this scale suggests potential gaps in the council's ability to prevent management override and unauthorised transactions.
findings.figures: Issue caused audit delays on management override testing in 2024/25
findings.quote: We identified a large volume of journals that did not individually balance to zero. Management invested a significant amount of time to resolve the issue, but ultimately it delayed our ability to progress this area in the timeframe available.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Plan and Strategy Memorandum (2025/26) – Staffordshire County Council
findings.headline: Auditor materiality increased to £22.1m based on expectation of increased undetected misstatements
findings.detail: The performance materiality range was increased from £18.8m to £22.1m for 2025/26, driven by auditor expectations of a higher level of undetected or uncorrected misstatements in the period. This is a negative signal about the expected control environment.
findings.matters: Rising materiality thresholds indicate the auditor has less confidence in the financial statements and expects more errors to slip through, meaning financial information is less reliable than in prior years.
findings.figures: Materiality range £22.1m (2024/25: £18.8m); misstatements threshold £1.7m (2024/25: £1.450m)
findings.quote: £22.1m driven by our expectations of increased level of undetected or uncorrected misstatements in the period

findings.paper_title: External Audit Plan and Strategy Memorandum (2025/26) – Staffordshire County Council
findings.headline: No substantive audit procedures performed at interim date due to prior-year control deficiencies
findings.detail: The auditor has explicitly stated they will not perform interim substantive procedures because of deficiencies identified in the previous year. This is an unusually cautious stance that signals the control environment was too weak to rely on in 2024/25.
findings.matters: This is an indicator that audit procedures cannot be split between interim and year-end work, suggesting material control weaknesses that require all testing to be done at period end when management has less time to remedy issues.
findings.figures: Interim procedures cancelled for entire 2025/26 audit
findings.quote: We will not perform any substantive procedures at an interim date due to the deficiencies identified in the previous year.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Plan and Strategy Memorandum (2025/26) – Staffordshire County Council
findings.headline: Approximately £180m of land and building assets had no valuation applied in 2024/25 audit
findings.detail: The auditor identified that while £147.1m was revalued and £395.4m received indexation uplift, approximately £180m of assets received no valuation adjustment at all. This represents a material control gap in the asset valuation process, predominantly operational land and buildings.
findings.matters: A balance sheet asset of this magnitude not being revalued creates uncertainty about whether the council's statement of financial position accurately reflects current values, a core concern for lenders assessing underlying asset security.
findings.figures: c£180m of unvalued assets, against total land and buildings of £670.5m subject to rolling revaluation
findings.quote: However, we identified c£180m of assets where no valuation was applied. This is predominantly operational land but there are also operational buildings valued on an Existing Use value basis.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Plan and Strategy Memorandum (2025/26) – Staffordshire County Council
findings.headline: Council has issued disclaimer opinions for three consecutive years and remains in rebuilding assurance phase
findings.detail: Staffordshire issued disclaimers for 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25. For 2025/26, the auditor is still completing a risk assessment as of 31 July 2026 before moving to substantive work. This indicates ongoing accounting control weaknesses that have not yet been resolved.
findings.matters: Multiple consecutive disclaimer opinions signal serious control environment deficiencies that would concern any potential lender about financial reporting reliability and the council's ability to maintain accurate accounts.
findings.figures: Three consecutive years of disclaimers (2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25)
findings.quote: We then issued a disclaimer of opinion for 2023/24 on 28 February 2025 and for 2024/25 on 27 February 2026 to comply with the statutory backstop date

findings.paper_title: 7. Agenda Item 7 (26 June 2026) Business Plan Outturn Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: Fund underperformed investment benchmark by 3.94 percentage points in 2025/26
findings.detail: The Staffordshire Pension Fund achieved an 8.90% total return in 2025/26 against its strategic benchmark of 12.84%, representing underperformance of 3.94 percentage points. This shortfall is predominantly attributed to active equity portfolio performance impacted by increased market concentration and volatility. However, the fund's longer-term annualized investment performance remains strong at over 7%, which exceeds the long-term investment return assumptions used by the Actuary in the triennial valuation.
findings.matters: Significant single-year investment underperformance against benchmark could signal strategy or manager issues, though the document attributes this to market conditions rather than fundamental management concerns.
findings.figures: 2025/26 fund return: 8.90% actual versus 12.84% benchmark; underperformance of 3.94 percentage points. Long-term annualized return exceeds 7%.
findings.quote: In 2025/26, the Fund's total investment return was 8.90% versus its strategic investment benchmark return of 12.84%, an underperformance of 3.94%, predominantly stemming from the Fund's active equity portfolios in response to an increase in market concentration and volatility.

findings.paper_title: 7. Agenda Item 7 (26 June 2026) Business Plan Outturn Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: Investment management fees anticipated to rise as private market allocations increase
findings.detail: Although 2025/26 investment management fees appear lower at £17.901m versus £20.702m in 2024/25, this reduction is temporary and driven by slower-than-expected private market drawdowns and a shift from active equities to fixed income. The report explicitly states that as the fund implements its approved Strategic Asset Allocation with increased allocations to private equity, private debt, infrastructure, and property, investment management costs will rise.
findings.matters: Planned expansion into more expensive private market asset classes represents a significant future cost escalation that will impact the council's pension fund contributions over coming years.
findings.figures: Investment management fees: £20.702m (2024/25) to £17.901m (2025/26); fund assets at 31 March 2026: £8.404bn.
findings.quote: Due to the outcome of the recent Strategic Asset Allocation review, where further allocations will be made to private market asset classes (private equity, private debt, infrastructure and property) it is anticipated the investment management costs will rise and will continue to be judged on a 'net return' basis.

findings.paper_title: 7. Agenda Item 7 (26 June 2026) Business Plan Outturn Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: LGPS Central pooling costs jumped 42% to £1.954m driven by regulatory compliance
findings.detail: The cost of participating in the LGPS Central asset pool increased from £1.378m to £1.954m, a rise of £576k or 42%. The report attributes this increase to additional costs relating to the Pensions Scheme Act 2026 and the 'Fit for the Future' government-mandated reforms. This category now represents the second-largest cost in the pension fund budget after investment management fees.
findings.matters: These cost increases are driven by government-mandated regulatory changes over which the council has no control, yet must fund as part of the mandatory pension pooling arrangement.
findings.figures: LGPS Central costs: £1.378m (2024/25) to £1.954m (2025/26), representing a £576k increase.
findings.quote: Total Oversight and Governance costs have increased in 2025/2026. This is principally due to the additional cost relating to LGPS Central and the increased budget sought in 2025/26 to fund the requirements of the 'Fit for the Future' reforms.

findings.headline: Energy cost savings reversed; council flagging downside risk to MTFS assumptions due to anticipated energy cost increases.
findings.detail: Central Accommodation achieved £1.0m saving in 2025/26 from lower gas and electricity usage and unit prices. However, only £0.750m is being built into the MTFS from 2026/27 onwards. The council explicitly notes further savings are unlikely, citing 'anticipated increased in energy costs linked to the conflict in the Middle East' as downside risk.
findings.matters: The council is flagging its own downside risk to MTFS assumptions. If energy costs increase materially, the council has identified £0.25m of at-risk savings, creating forward pressure on the Medium-Term Financial Strategy.
findings.figures: £1.0m saving 2025/26; £0.75m taken as recurring MTFS saving; £0.25m flagged as at-risk
findings.quote: Any further contribution to the MTFS will be closely monitored in 2026/27 but this is deemed unlikely at the moment due to anticipated increased in energy costs linked to the conflict in the Middle East.

findings.headline: Children in Care placement costs £3.8m overbudget with numbers rising; council using reserves unsustainably to mask control issues.
findings.detail: Placement costs are £3.762m overbudget from rising placements through the year (1,363 children in care by end March). Family Safeguarding overspent by £2.430m on agency and Section 17 spend. Overall Children & Families achieved breakeven only by drawing £4.560m from reserves. The council explicitly states this drawdown 'is unsustainable in the long term' and acknowledged 'significant failings were identified through 2019-22 and most recently in 2023'. A £5.5m investment across two years has been approved for service restructure.
findings.matters: Using £4.6m annually to offset service overspends masks control and performance issues. The council has explicitly flagged unsustainability and acknowledged repeated service failures, creating risk that savings targets in the MTFS will not be achieved.
findings.figures: CiC placement costs £3.762m overbudget; Family Safeguarding £2.430m overspend; reserves used £4.560m to achieve breakeven; £5.500m phased investment approved
findings.quote: This has been offset this year by additional use of reserves, totalling £2.500m; however, this is unsustainable in the long term and, given existing CiC numbers, there is a significant risk that target savings over the period of the MTFS will not be fully achieved.

findings.headline: Adult social care cost pressures sustained at £7.1m; client debt significantly above target at £26.1m, indicating affordability and collection challenges.
findings.detail: Care Commissioning reports £0.977m net overspend, with Older People placements £7.135m overbudget and Learning Disability £2.018m overbudget. These are funded from the Health and Care risk reserve; £5.107m drawn this year. Health and Care Client debt now stands at £26.086m, exceeding the 2025/26 target of £23.715m by £2.371m. The Cost Recovery Plan is reducing placement costs but pressures remain recurrent.
findings.matters: Recurring care cost pressures are eroding the Health and Care risk reserve, which has limited capacity. Deteriorating client debt collection in this vulnerable population suggests either service affordability issues or collection challenges that constrain future recovery.
findings.figures: Care Commissioning net overspend £0.977m; Older People £7.135m overbudget; Learning Disability £2.018m overbudget; Health and Care risk reserve draw £5.107m; client debt £2.371m above target
findings.quote: After taking account of all mitigating actions and favourable variances across Care Commissioning totalling £2.994m, the remaining balance of cost pressures totals £5.107m which is funded from the Health and Care risk reserve.

findings.headline: SEND High Needs Block deficit worsened to £94.4m, driven by placement costs and complexity of need; ringfenced and dependent on Government support.
findings.detail: The High Needs Block overspent by £43.6m in 2025/26. The underlying DSG reserve deficit has deepened from £53.6m (end 2024/25) to £94.4m (end 2025/26). New independent special school placements are averaging £0.070m per annum and numbers have doubled in four years. The deficit is ringfenced under statutory override through 2027/28. The council states the position 'will take time and is unlikely to address in full the worsening position without further Government support'.
findings.matters: This structural deficit cannot be absorbed into general balances and is beyond the council's control to solve. It represents a material call on resources that cannot be redirected and is dependent on Government intervention.
findings.figures: £43.6m overspend; DSG reserve deficit £94.4m (up from £53.6m); new placements averaging £0.070m p.a.; placement numbers double those of four years ago
findings.quote: For 2025/26 the High Needs Block is overspent by £43.6m and reflects both continuing growing demand for SEND support and increasing complexity of need and costs... This will take time and is unlikely to address in full the worsening position without further Government support

findings.headline: Mandatory biodiversity net gain requirement identified as cost pressure on major school construction projects
findings.detail: From February 2024, all major developments require demonstrating 10% biodiversity net gain. The council has identified this as a cost pressure but has not yet quantified its impact on individual projects.
findings.matters: BNG obligations will increase construction costs; impacts project budgets and may delay delivery if not anticipated.
findings.figures: 10% biodiversity net gain requirement
findings.quote: From 12 February 2024, it became mandatory for all major developments requiring planning permission to demonstrate a BNG of 10%… Meeting BNG obligations will be a further cost pressure.

findings.headline: Capital programme over-programmed by £603k, relying on achieving procurement savings to balance budget
findings.detail: Programme totals £27.26m against available funding of £26.66m. The council plans to bring forward £603,760 of additional works to offset expected slippage, financing the overspend from procurement savings with deferred provision in 2027/28 if savings are not achieved.
findings.matters: Budget balance depends on achieving cost savings in procurement; if not achieved, shortfall defers to next year, creating risk of programme compression.
findings.figures: £603,760 over-programming against £26,659,698 available funding; total programme £27,263,458
findings.quote: There are provisional plans to bring forward £603,760 of works above an overall programme of £26,659,698 in 2026/27. These provisions are based on previous years programme performance and the intention is to finance some of the advance spend from savings made in procuring the programme. Provision will be made in 2027/28 to finance any outstanding balance.

findings.headline: SEND population growing year-on-year, with above-average reliance on expensive independent provision
findings.detail: EHCP numbers are circa 9,925 (Jan 2026) and continue to increase. Unlike the 7% national and West Midlands average, 10% of Staffordshire's EHCP pupils attend independent or non-maintained special schools—suggesting the council faces higher-cost placements. The SEND capital programme for 2026/27 is £9.7m.
findings.matters: Above-average reliance on independent provision signals persistent cost pressures; growing EHCP numbers suggest sustained capital and revenue demand.
findings.figures: 9,925 EHCP pupils, 10% in independent provision vs 7% national/West Midlands average
findings.quote: SCC currently maintains EHCPs for circa 9,925 children and young people (January 2026). The proportion of children with an EHCP continues to increase year-on-year. In Staffordshire, 10% of children and young people with an EHCP attend an independent or non-maintained special school. This is above both the national and West Midlands averages, which stand at 7%.

findings.headline: School Condition Allocation funding is estimated; programme requires review when government confirms allocation
findings.detail: The £4.5m School Condition Allocation (SCA) funding is currently estimated. The council awaits formal DfE confirmation and has flagged that the capital programme will need to be reviewed for affordability once the actual allocation is announced.
findings.matters: A shortfall in SCA allocation would force immediate reprioritisation of maintained school investment.
findings.figures: £4.5m (estimated)
findings.quote: We await DfE confirmation of our 2026/27 allocation, therefore the School's Capital Programme is based on an estimated SCA of £4.5m. The programme will need to be reviewed once the funding allocation is announced to ensure affordability.

findings.headline: Climate change will force additional investment in highway resilience, but the cost is unquantified and not yet budgeted
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that extreme weather is already affecting the network (flooding, wind, heat, extreme winter), and that 'this may require changes to the way roads are designed and managed to ensure an appropriate degree of resilience. This will come at an additional cost that requires a detailed understanding of the predicted likely future impacts of more impactful weather.' No cost estimate or timeline is provided.
findings.matters: An emerging cost pressure known to the council but not yet quantified is likely to create budget pressures in future years
findings.figures: Cost unquantified; no timeline given
findings.quote: This will come at an additional cost that requires a detailed understanding of the predicted likely future impacts of more impactful weather.

findings.headline: The council is recruiting staff and buying systems with one-off revenue funding, and has budgeted for redundancy costs if the funding disappears
findings.detail: Staffordshire received £4.074m Local Transport Grant revenue resource to fill capacity and capability gaps. A resource-gap analysis found that 'the business-as-usual work model is not enabling us to achieve the desired outcomes.' The council plans to use the funding for new FTE positions and technology. Explicitly: 'Where recruitment takes place, funding will be set aside to cover any potential redundancy costs if the Government reduce or remove the funding in future years.'
findings.matters: Building staffing and systems on temporary funding creates a future liability if funding ends; this suggests the council recognises a real risk of service disruption or stranded costs
findings.figures: £4.074m revenue resource; available through 2028/29 for revenue
findings.quote: Where recruitment takes place, funding will be set aside to cover any potential redundancy costs if the Government reduce or remove the funding in future years, therefore protecting the County Council from this liability.

findings.headline: Department for Transport rated Staffordshire's road maintenance Amber, not meeting national standards
findings.detail: The DfT's 2026 Local Highways Maintenance Transparency Report assessed Staffordshire across condition, spend, and best-practice criteria and assigned an Amber rating. While the council formally disputes the rating, it acknowledges that it must demonstrate better value and best practice to improve to Green.
findings.matters: An independent audit finding of substandard asset management suggests operational or strategic deficiencies; future funding could be jeopardised if the council cannot improve its rating
findings.figures: Amber rating (target: Green)
findings.quote: This year, Staffordshire County Council has been rated Amber. While the DfT's interpretation of the submitted data has not been applied consistently across authorities and the Council has formally recorded that it does not agree with the Amber rating, it is nevertheless clear that, in future, we must demonstrate more explicitly the best practice being applied and the value being achieved in order to secure a Green rating.

findings.headline: Government funding covers only 40% of what's needed to maintain a £56m-per-annum asset, and a repair backlog is mounting
findings.detail: The council's carriageway asset needs £56m per annum to maintain in steady state. DfT funding is significantly below this level. The council is bridging part of the gap with its own money (£7.5m per year for two years), but acknowledges that despite this support, 'there is a mounting repair backlog.' The council notes that the £8 billion network replacement value far exceeds available government allocation.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether unfunded maintenance obligations will accumulate into a future liability, or whether the council can sustain this gap indefinitely
findings.figures: £56m per annum required; government funding 'significantly below' this; £7.5m council contribution for 2026/27–2027/28; £8 billion network replacement value
findings.quote: the annual investment required to maintain the carriageway asset alone in a steady state is estimated to be at least £56m per annum. DfT funding is significantly below this level and, despite additional support from the council, there is a mounting repair backlog.

findings.paper_title: 6. Agenda Item 6 (3 March 2026) Pensions Annual Investment Strategy for Cash
findings.headline: Pensions Bill reform from April 2026 will split pension fund cash management between the council and LGPS Central, with implementation details still uncertain.
findings.detail: The government's Pensions Bill will divide the pension fund's cash into 'operational cash' managed by the council and 'investment cash' managed by LGPS Central. The council acknowledges 'much uncertainty on how it will work in practice' and commits to informing the Pensions Panel of any changes to approach throughout 2026/27. The 2026/27 strategy is being prepared on current principles pending regulatory clarity.
findings.matters: A material regulatory change affecting pension fund governance is imminent with uncertain implementation. Lenders need to understand how regulatory change will affect fund management and whether it creates operational or financial risks.
findings.figures: Cash strategic allocation is 1.0% of the Staffordshire Pension Fund.
findings.quote: The upcoming Pensions Bill implementing the Governments' Fit for the Future' reforms from April 2026, will have huge implications for how the Fund's cash is managed.

findings.headline: Financing costs rising from 3.0% to 3.4% of net revenue
findings.detail: The proportion of net revenue stream consumed by financing costs is forecast to increase from 3.0% to 3.4%, while absolute financing costs rise from £22.0m to £25.1m. Debt servicing is growing faster than revenue.
findings.matters: For a lender, an increasing financing cost ratio indicates the council's capacity to service debt and take on additional borrowing is tightening. This is a key creditworthiness indicator.
findings.figures: 3.0% budget to 3.4% forecast; £22.0m to £25.1m
findings.quote: Proportion of financing costs to net revenue stream – Proportion of Net Revenue Stream - % 3.0% 3.4%

findings.headline: Long-term investments cut 88% from £245m budget to £30m forecast
findings.detail: The upper limit for principal sums invested for longer than a year has fallen dramatically from £245.0m in the budget to only £30m in the forecast. This £215m reduction represents either a major shift in treasury strategy, a drawdown of reserves, or changed cash circumstances.
findings.matters: For a lender, a sharp reduction in longer-term investments signals either planned reserve depletion or financial stress. It directly affects the council's liquidity and financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £245.0m budgeted, £30m forecast
findings.quote: Upper limit for total principal sums invested for longer than a year 245.0 30

findings.headline: Long-term investment limit revised down from £245m budget to £30m forecast
findings.detail: The upper limit for principal sums invested for longer than a year is forecast at £30m, against a budgeted £245m. This £215m reduction suggests the council is retaining cash rather than investing it, a substantial shift from planned deployment of funds.
findings.matters: A sharp reduction in long-term investment signals the council may be prioritizing liquidity over returns, which could indicate underlying cash flow concerns not evident in headline figures.
findings.figures: £245m budget vs £30m forecast
findings.quote: Upper limit for total principal sums invested for longer than a year 245.0 30

findings.headline: External debt loans forecast at £340m, significantly below the £510m budget
findings.detail: Loans are forecast at £340m compared to a budgeted £510m—a reduction of £170m (33%). Despite capital expenditure remaining close to plan (£131m forecast vs £135.2m budgeted), borrowing is materially lower, suggesting either deferred capital schemes or greater use of existing cash reserves.
findings.matters: A material downward revision in external borrowing requires explanation; it may indicate either improved cash generation (positive) or forced deferral of planned investments due to cash constraints (concerning).
findings.figures: £510m budget vs £340m forecast
findings.quote: External Debt - Loans 510 340

findings.headline: Financing costs forecast at 3.4% of net revenue stream, above the 3.0% budgeted target
findings.detail: Financing costs are forecast at £25.1m against a budget of £22.0m, representing a £3.1m increase. As a proportion of net revenue stream, this rises from 3.0% to 3.4%. This 0.4 percentage point increase means more of the council's revenue is committed to debt servicing than anticipated.
findings.matters: Higher-than-expected debt servicing costs reduce the council's financial flexibility and indicate either adverse interest rate movements or borrowing at higher rates than planned, constraining capacity for additional debt.
findings.figures: Financing costs £25.1m (forecast) vs £22.0m (budget); proportion 3.4% vs 3.0%
findings.quote: Proportion of financing costs to net revenue stream – Proportion of Net Revenue Stream - % 3.0% 3.4%

findings.paper_title: Audit Results Report - Staffordshire County Council - Final Version
findings.headline: Audit remains incomplete; auditor cannot yet certify completion due to prior-year certificate, WGA instructions, and outstanding matters.
findings.detail: As of the audit committee meeting on 17 February 2026, KPMG's audit is not fully complete. The team cannot certify the audit as complete pending: prior year certificate; Whole of Government Accounts (WGA) instructions from the NAO (not yet received); and resolution of outstanding matters. This extends audit risk into the post-accounts publication period.
findings.matters: An uncertified audit that extends beyond publication of accounts creates uncertainty about whether further adjustments may be required and signals additional audit risk or process delays.
findings.figures: Audit completion date: pending. Backstop: 27 February 2026 (now passed as of audit report date). Meeting date: 17 February 2026.
findings.quote: The following work is outstanding to allow us to certify the audit: Prior year certificate; Whole of Government Accounts; and confirmation from the National Audit Office that their audit of the Whole of Government Accounts is complete

findings.paper_title: Audit Results Report - Staffordshire County Council - Final Version
findings.headline: Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP) completion rate of 48% is below statutory requirement (20-week target) and below national average of 46.4%.
findings.detail: Staffordshire is failing to meet the statutory 20-week target for EHCP completion set by the Children and Families Act 2024. In 2024/25, only 48% of plans were completed on time (council target was 48%, a 'realistic target' but below the legal requirement). This is a governance concern regarding statutory compliance in a significant service area. Management recognizes it as 'one of the top performance challenges for 2025-26' and has committed additional resource.
findings.matters: Failure to meet statutory EHCP timelines exposes the council to legal challenge and signals governance weakness. SEND services are expensive; delays compound costs and indicate resource/process problems.
findings.figures: 48% completion rate against 20-week statutory requirement (effectively 100%); national average 46.4%; prior year 50.3%; Q2 2024/25 achieved 55.7%
findings.quote: Following review of the integrated performance reports, Staffordshire is also failing to meet these timeframes and is performing lower than the national average. It has set itself a target of 48% in 24-25, this considered a realistic target but still one which is below the statutory requirement.

findings.paper_title: Audit Results Report - Staffordshire County Council - Final Version
findings.headline: Three significant control deficiencies and five other control deficiencies identified; no segregation of duties over journal posting.
findings.detail: Auditor identified multiple control weaknesses including: absence of formal control reviewing valuer assumptions for property (risk relates to £180m valuation gap); no segregation of duties over journal entries; journals not reviewed or approved before posting. Management accepted residual risk on the journal control in prior year and this remains unresolved. These deficiencies respond to significant risks but management views them as acceptable.
findings.matters: Control deficiencies in core financial processes (journals, fixed assets) indicate the council's internal control environment has structural gaps that supervisory controls may not adequately mitigate.
findings.figures: 3 significant control deficiencies; 5 other control deficiencies; prior year control deficiencies partially remediated (only 5 of prior issues addressed)
findings.quote: Journals are not reviewed or approved before being posted and there is a risk that journals could be posted erroneously or inappropriately. We raised this deficiency in the prior year and noted that management accepted the residual risk.

findings.paper_title: Audit Results Report - Staffordshire County Council - Final Version
findings.headline: Management incorrectly recognized £7.4 million Right of Use asset on a peppercorn lease with no corresponding liability under IFRS 16.
findings.detail: On early adoption of IFRS 16 in 2023/24 (formal requirement from 1 April 2024), the Council recorded a £7.4m Right of Use asset for a peppercorn lease but did not record the corresponding lease liability. This was identified during audit and corrected by management. Auditor was unable to complete all lease procedures due to backstop deadline constraints.
findings.matters: IFRS 16 implementation errors indicate incomplete financial statement controls and knowledge of new accounting standards. A £7.4m misstatement (even if corrected) suggests other lease errors may remain undetected.
findings.figures: £7.4 million Right of Use asset incorrectly recognized
findings.quote: Management incorrectly recognized a £7.4m Right of Use asset. This had no corresponding lease liability as it was a peppercorn lease. The note has been adjusted by management.

findings.paper_title: Audit Results Report - Staffordshire County Council - Final Version
findings.headline: Pension liability decreased by £329.7 million year-on-year to £2,029 million, driven by market conditions moving councils into surplus.
findings.detail: The Council's Local Government Pension Scheme funded liability fell significantly from £2,358.7m to £2,029m. Auditor completed detailed testing of actuarial assumptions (discount rate, inflation, mortality) and found them overall balanced, with mortality assumptions cautious compared to auditor's central rates. Auditor notes this is consistent with sector-wide movement into pension surpluses due to market changes, which creates complex accounting questions under IFRS standards.
findings.matters: A £330m swing in pension liabilities affects both the balance sheet position and the credibility of long-term financial planning. A council moving from significant deficit to surplus changes its refinancing risk profile materially.
findings.figures: £2,029m at 31 March 2025 (down £329.7m from prior year). Actuarial assumptions assessed as 'balanced overall'.
findings.quote: recent changes to market conditions have meant that more councils are finding themselves moving into surplus in their Local Government Pension Scheme (or surpluses have grown and have become material). The requirements of the accounting standards on recognition of these surplus are complicated and requires actuarial involvement.

findings.paper_title: Audit Results Report - Staffordshire County Council - Final Version
findings.headline: Journal posting system processes approximately 500,000 unbalanced transaction lines, indicating control weakness in the general ledger.
findings.detail: During audit testing, KPMG identified a large volume of journals that did not individually balance to zero. Investigation revealed this is because corresponding debit and credit entries are generated from different feeder systems and carry separate journal reference numbers. Management spent significant time updating transaction listings to evidence reconciliation, delaying audit procedures. Auditor raised a formal recommendation on page 31 (not detailed in this extract) and will discuss fee variations for additional effort required.
findings.matters: Journal processing problems can mask fraudulent entries, errors in expense coding, or misallocations between cost centres. The scale (500k lines) and the delays it caused are red flags for control environment quality.
findings.figures: Approximately 500,000 transaction lines; multiple feeder systems involved; 'multiple discussions and meetings' required to resolve
findings.quote: During our work on journals, we identified a large volume of journals that did not individually balance to zero. Given the nature and volume of these entries (c500k transaction lines), additional audit effort was required to understand the underlying journal posting process.

findings.paper_title: Audit Results Report - Staffordshire County Council - Final Version
findings.headline: £180 million of land and building assets have received no valuation at year-end, creating a material valuation gap.
findings.detail: The Council values property on a rolling 5-year cycle. Only £147.1m was revalued by the external valuer (DVS), with £395.4m uplifted by desktop indices. However, approximately £180m of assets — predominantly operational land but including operational buildings — received no valuation adjustment at all. Auditor has recommended management prepare an annual paper evidencing satisfaction that these unvalued assets are free from material misstatement.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the actual value of the council's property assets. A £180m gap in valuation methodology is a control deficiency affecting balance sheet reliability.
findings.figures: £147.1m valued by DVS; £395.4m uplifted via desktop indices; c£180m with no valuation applied
findings.quote: We identified there is a significant proportion of land and building assets which are not subject to any valuation at the balance sheet date. The DVS value assets on a rolling valuation basis, this year valuing £147.1m. Finance then applied a desktop indices uplift to £395.4m of assets valued on a depreciated replacement cost (DRC) basis (not included in the DVS valuation exercise). However, we identified c£180m of assets where no valuation was applied.

findings.paper_title: Audit Results Report - Staffordshire County Council - Final Version
findings.headline: Auditor has disclaimed opinion on financial statements due to inability to complete sufficient audit work before statutory deadline.
findings.detail: KPMG cannot certify the accounts. Due to the statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026, they lack sufficient audit evidence on key areas including the split of usable/unusable reserves (deemed pervasive to the Council's financial position), land and buildings valuations, PFI and lease liabilities, infrastructure assets, and employee benefit expenses. This is the second consecutive disclaimer for this council.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion signals the council's financial position cannot be verified by its external auditor. This directly affects the credibility of published accounts and any borrowing decisions based on them.
findings.figures: Backstop deadline 27 February 2026. Prior year also disclaimed. 2023/24 audit similarly disclaimed.
findings.quote: we have determined that there is insufficient time to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the split of useable and unusable reserves as at 31 March 2025 or 31 March 2024 ahead of the backstop, and, in our view, this is pervasive to the Council's financial position as at 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: ISA 260 Staffordshire Final Pension Fund Committee
findings.headline: The £546.1 million directly held property portfolio lacks independent management review of valuations, creating audit risk
findings.detail: While the fund appoints Savills to value the property portfolio, KPMG found no formal management review or control meeting audit standards for this significant risk area. One property sample (29 Avro Way) was initially valued £1.9 million above the acceptable range, though this was below materiality. Management has since established quarterly oversight meetings with Colliers and Savills.
findings.matters: Direct property holdings represent 7.1% of pension fund assets; lack of independent management review creates material valuation risk that could affect reported pension liabilities.
findings.figures: Direct property holdings £546.1m (9.6 times performance materiality); one property sample overstated by £1,900,000
findings.quote: Whilst the Trustee appoints a third party (Savills) to value the property, we did not identify an associated management review or other control that meets the requirements of the auditing standards.

findings.paper_title: ISA 260 Staffordshire Final Pension Fund Committee
findings.headline: Journal entry authorization controls do not meet audit standards, though management disputes the assessment
findings.detail: KPMG identified that the pension fund's journal review process, while documented by management, lacks formal authorization procedures, clear approval authority, and formal recording of review conclusions. Management disagreed, stating that existing controls within the finance system and delegation framework are sufficient. KPMG examined 7 high-risk journal entries and found no unauthorized entries in their current work.
findings.matters: Weak controls over journal entry authorization increase the risk of undetected errors or unauthorized adjustments to financial statements, which affects the reliability of reported financial position.
findings.figures: 7 high-risk journal entries examined; no unauthorized entries identified to date
findings.quote: Despite management's evidence of a review process, it does not fully meet the rigorous standards required. To improve journal controls, management should thoroughly document the review process, ensuring each journal entry is accurate and justified, and formally record review outcomes.

findings.paper_title: ISA 260 Staffordshire Final Pension Fund Committee
findings.headline: £19.4 million valuation adjustment to Level 3 pooled investments indicates a weakness in the pension fund's investment control process
findings.detail: KPMG identified a net overstatement of £19.4 million in Level 3 pooled investment vehicles between the draft financial statements and the investment manager valuation statements. This was corrected in the final version following receipt of updated information from investment managers. Level 3 investments represent 23.6% of the fund's £7,727.7 million portfolio and rely on unobservable inputs for valuation.
findings.matters: Material valuation adjustments to pension assets directly affect the reported size of the fund's liabilities and the council's long-term financial obligations, which lenders and finance directors need to understand when assessing the council's financial position.
findings.figures: £19,447k net overstatement; Level 3 investments £1,824.7m of £7,727.7m total (23.6% of portfolio)
findings.quote: We noted a net overstatement of £19,447k in investments, which is the variance between the valuations as per the pension fund financial statements and those as per investment manager valuation statements. The misstatement has been corrected in the final draft financial statements.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation 2028 creates mid-MTFS uncertainty and risk of saving plan disruption
findings.detail: LGR is expected during 2028, 'part way through the MTFS period, adding additional uncertainty.' The council identifies a 'financial risk that the implementation of LGR part way through the MTFS process could see disruption to saving plans within the MTFS as the organisation's focus might be prioritised elsewhere.' Final government decision expected summer 2026, with earliest operational changes expected 2028.
findings.matters: Structural reorganisation mid-planning period creates execution risk for savings delivery at the exact moment when structural deficits are emerging, potentially making the underlying deficit position worse than currently forecast.
findings.figures: LGR operational changes expected 2028, government decision expected summer 2026
findings.quote: There is a financial risk that the implementation of LGR part way through the MTFS process could see disruption to saving plans within the MTFS as the organisation's focus might be prioritised elsewhere.

findings.headline: Commercial investment strategy approved for up to £10m additional investment in 2026/27, on top of existing commitments
findings.detail: Council approved 'a maximum quantum for commercial investments of a further £10 million in 2026/27' and 'a maximum limit for an individual service investment loan of £20 million in 2026/27.' Any upwards changes are delegated to the Director of Finance. This represents discretionary capital deployment at a time when the council faces structural budget gaps and rising demand pressures.
findings.matters: Continued expansion of commercial investments during a period of budget deficit and DSG crisis suggests management confidence in investment returns, but also concentration of risk if market conditions deteriorate or investments underperform.
findings.figures: £10m maximum quantum for new commercial investments, £20m maximum individual service investment loan limit
findings.quote: Approve a maximum quantum for commercial investments of a further £10 million in 2026/27

findings.headline: Council tax rising 3.99% to fund structural spending gap, with no growth in central government funding
findings.detail: The proposed 2026/27 council tax increase is 3.99% (2.00% Adult Social Care precept + 1.99% general precept). However, the Fair Funding Review settlement is 'broadly cash flat' at £311.707m in 2026/27, 'shows that there is no growth in funding from central government in that period either, putting more pressure on increasing council tax to generate an increase in revenue streams in future years.' From 2027/28, planning assumes only 2.99% council tax increases.
findings.matters: Reliance on above-inflation council tax rises to fund spending, combined with flat central grant, indicates residents are bearing the cost of service pressures. Persistent above-inflation rises risk council tax collection issues and political resistance, while fixed grant income limits the council's revenue flexibility.
findings.figures: 3.99% increase for 2026/27 (£64.71 per annum for Band D taxpayer at £1,686.42), £311.707m cash flat core spending power
findings.quote: Although this provides certainty over funding for the next 3 years it also shows that there is no growth in funding from central government in that period either, putting more pressure on increasing council tax to generate an increase in revenue streams in future years.

findings.headline: Adult social care facing sustained cost pressures from National Living Wage and care home fee inflation beyond planned uplifts
findings.detail: Health and Care Directorate faces 'cost pressures due to rising demand from an ageing population as well as rising prices, in part as a result of increases in the National Living Wage.' Notably, 'care home prices continuing to rise over and above planned fee uplifts' in 2024/25 and early 2025/26, plus 'impact of the NHS Operational Plan, which has shifted some costs to the Council' and 'high-cost care for some individuals.'
findings.matters: Uncontrollable external cost drivers (wage inflation, care provider pricing) forcing ad-hoc budget pressures indicate the council faces ongoing in-year overspends that cannot be managed through savings targets, increasing reliance on contingency and reserves.
findings.figures: No specific quantified pressure given in this excerpt, but identified as 'particularly significant' in late 2024/25 and early 2025/26
findings.quote: Cost pressures have been particularly significant towards the end of 2024/25 and early in 2025/26 with care home prices continuing to rise over and above planned fee uplifts, the impact of the NHS Operational Plan, which has shifted some costs to the Council, and high-cost care for some individuals.

findings.headline: Children's social care numbers rising beyond MTFS assumptions with escalating placement costs
findings.detail: The Children and Families Directorate is experiencing 'increasing numbers of children in our care' with 'increasing cost of placements'. The document explicitly notes 'the number of children needing our help is increasing beyond the levels which are assumed in the MTFS, this is a significant risk that needs to be managed moving forwards.' A pressure of up to £5.5m by 2027/28 has been added for early intervention, reflecting inability to manage within current budget.
findings.matters: Demographic and demand pressures exceeding budget assumptions indicate the council cannot control spending growth through current interventions, with direct risk to budget delivery and potential need for emergency service reductions or cuts elsewhere.
findings.figures: £5.5m pressure by 2027/28 for early intervention programmes
findings.quote: However, the number of children needing our help is increasing beyond the levels which are assumed in the MTFS, this is a significant risk that needs to be managed moving forwards.

findings.headline: General balances depleted over MTFS period despite risk assessment requiring £60m+
findings.detail: General balances are currently £62.2m and planned contributions of £3.688m for 2026/27 (along with previously approved usage) will draw this down to £56.6m by 2028/29. The risk assessment concludes 'in excess of £60m is deemed to be an appropriate level' given increased risks in social care, children's services, and LGR uncertainty. The depletion leaves the council operating near minimum prudent reserves with rising pressures.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves toward minimum levels while facing escalating structural deficits reduces the council's buffer against unexpected shocks and limits its ability to manage the DSG deficit or service volatility without seeking emergency borrowing.
findings.figures: £62.2m current general balances, £56.6m by 2028/29, £60m+ assessed as appropriate minimum
findings.quote: These contributions will then be drawn down and used to balance the budgets in the years 2026/27 to 2028/29, as approved in the 2024/25 MTFS, leaving the level of general balances at £56.6m by 2028/29.

findings.headline: Structural budget gaps emerge from 2027/28 onwards despite 2026/27 being balanced
findings.detail: While 2026/27 is balanced, the MTFS shows 'gaps in every future year' of the plan. The document explicitly states that 'significant gaps emerge' from 2028/29 onwards when the previously approved use of reserves becomes 'not sustainable'. Net movement pressures escalate from £37.981m in 2026/27 to £156.637m by 2030/31.
findings.matters: The council is managing short-term balance through unsustainable reserve drawdown while structural pressures remain unaddressed, indicating potential difficulty in delivering savings targets or service cuts needed to balance future years.
findings.quote: The graph shows a balanced position for 2026/27 with gaps in every future year of the MTFS.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit forecast to reach £500m by end of MTFS, with no clear mitigation
findings.detail: The High Needs Block is forecast to overspend by £42m in the current year. The DSG reserve, already £53.6m in deficit at end of 2024/25, is forecast to reach over £90m in deficit by end of 2025/26. The council's deficit management plan 'does not appear to have had any significant impact' and the unmitigated forecast shows the deficit could reach £500m by end of MTFS. This is driven by doubling of numbers in independent sector placements and rising complexity of need.
findings.matters: A £500m DSG deficit represents an unsustainable liability that will eventually require funding from council reserves or central government intervention, directly threatening the council's financial sustainability and the lender's ability to recover.
findings.figures: £53.6m deficit at end 2024/25, forecast over £90m by end 2025/26, £500m forecast by end MTFS period, £42m High Needs Block overspend forecast in current year
findings.quote: The current forecast of the deficit, without any mitigations shows around £500m could be reached by the end of the MTFS period.

findings.paper_title: Half Yearly Treasury Management Report for the period ended 30 September 2025
findings.headline: Internal cash reserves used to fund capital programmes instead of external borrowing, generating £1 million interest savings in six months
findings.detail: The council holds cash balances ranging from £417 million to £541 million and is deliberately funding operations and capital from these reserves rather than external borrowing. The strategy is predicated on investment returns remaining lower than borrowing costs. The council estimates £1 million in interest cost reductions for the first half of the year.
findings.matters: This strategy reduces interest costs but depends on the rate environment remaining favourable and creates a vulnerability if cash reserves are deployed elsewhere or if rates move unfavourably.
findings.figures: £1 million estimated interest savings in first half 2025/26; cash balances ranged between £417 million and £541 million; external loan portfolio £355.5 million
findings.quote: Internally funding from cash balances in lieu of borrowing is reducing the average interest paid on County Council debt and is estimated to have saved £1 million in interest payments in the first half of the financial year.

findings.paper_title: Half Yearly Treasury Management Report for the period ended 30 September 2025
findings.headline: £15 million LOBO loan repaid early after lender exercised call option with rate increase to 7.29%
findings.detail: The council repaid a LOBO loan in the first half of 2025/26 when the lender exercised their call option and increased the interest rate from 4.275% to 7.29%. Two remaining LOBO loans totalling £18 million remain on the balance sheet with imminent call dates: £10m callable on 11 December 2025 and £8m on 30 January 2026, creating refinancing risk in the second half of the year.
findings.matters: LOBO loans create forced refinancing risk when lenders exercise call options. The imminent call dates on the remaining loans could force the council into material refinancing decisions in a rising rate environment.
findings.figures: £15 million LOBO loan repaid; interest rate increased from 4.275% to 7.29%; £18 million LOBO loans remain with call dates 11/12/2025 and 30/01/2026
findings.quote: During the first six months of the year the County Council repaid a £15 million LOBO loan early due to the lender exercising their call options and increasing the interest rate payable on the loan from 4.275% to 7.29%.

findings.headline: Care fee uplift proposed at 3.6% in 2026/27 to address provider market pressures and sufficiency risk
findings.detail: The working group noted that discretionary fee uplift was already budgeted at only 2.72% but recommended increasing to 3.6% to reflect actual cost pressures (National Living Wage 4.1%, CPI 2.3%). This needs balancing against other MTFS priorities. If uplift is insufficient, care providers may pass costs to residents or decline to take new SCC placements.
findings.matters: Inadequate fee uplifts risk care market sufficiency and may force residents onto private rates. This is both a social care risk and a financial risk if costs escalate when capacity becomes constrained.
findings.figures: Current MTFS uplift 2.72%; recommended uplift 3.6%; National Living Wage forecast increase 4.1%
findings.quote: The MTFS currently includes funding for an overall fee uplift of 2.72%; it will be recommended that this is increased to 3.6%, however, this will need to be considered in the context of other priorities.

findings.headline: Adult social care workforce vacancies at 9.3% with 26.2% turnover; 6% indirectly employed through agencies at £18-19/hour
findings.detail: Social care provider vacancies are high and turnover is substantial, with agencies filling gaps at premium rates. A national fair pay agreement in adult social care would further increase costs for care providers. Workforce retention is identified as a challenge with no career path for care workers.
findings.matters: High agency spend and turnover increase unit costs and service volatility. This adds to care price pressures and supply risk in a market already stressed.
findings.figures: Vacancies 9.3%; turnover 26.2%; 6% indirectly employed; agency rate £18-19/hour
findings.quote: Currently vacancies sit at 9.3%, with turnover of staff at 26.2% and 6% indirectly employed, including through agencies. Agency staff are typically paid a higher rate - around £18-19 per hour.

findings.headline: NHS cost shifting: Continuing Healthcare (CHC) cost pressure of £3.5m identified, with NHS reducing CHC placements onto council
findings.detail: The NHS Integrated Care Board (ICB) has targeted £306m in savings including reductions in Continuing Healthcare numbers. The council has identified a cost pressure of £3.5m from NHS reducing CHC placements, with potential for this to rise. The full impact of NHS staff reductions on adult social care is not yet assessed.
findings.matters: This is cost shunting from the health service to the local authority at a time when adult social care is already under severe pressure. The NHS operational plan is not yet finalised, so the full exposure is unknown.
findings.figures: £3.5M cost pressure identified so far from CHC reductions; ICB targeting £306m in savings
