findings.quote: the NHS and Council are working on referral pathways however there is a cost pressure from the NHS reducing the number of people on CHC – estimated at around £3.5M so far this year and potentially rising in future years.

findings.headline: Budget balanced for 2026/27 only; considerable savings programme required from 2027/28 onwards if council tax remains at assumed 2.99%
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget is set at 3.99% council tax increase (below the 4.99% maximum). This compresses the MTFS from three years of balance to one year. From 2027/28, if council tax remains at the assumed 2.99% increase, the council faces a significant savings gap that has not yet been fully identified and costed.
findings.matters: A one-year balanced budget reveals structural deficit pressure. The council's ability to identify and deliver the required savings from 2027/28 is unproven, and efficiency reviews remain incomplete.
findings.figures: £21.4m savings in 2026/27 budget; council tax increase 3.99% (below 4.99% maximum)
findings.quote: The 3.99% increase this year has impact on the remainder of the MTFS, which will go from three years balanced budget to a one-year balanced budget and a considerable savings programme in 2027/28 and future years if the CT remains at the currently assumed 2.99%.

findings.headline: Highways funding covers only 60% of steady-state maintenance requirement; structural deterioration accelerating
findings.detail: Current funding provides approximately £6m annually for structures when annual depreciation is £21m. The gross replacement cost to eliminate the current backlog is £1.873bn. Over the next five years, average road bridge condition is predicted to fall 4.7%, with critical load-bearing elements falling 1.0%. The council is lobbying for multi-year settlements but one-year government funding limits effective planning.
findings.matters: An essential asset base is deteriorating on a known trajectory with insufficient capital to arrest it. This becomes a service and reputational risk, and forces reactive spending later at higher cost.
findings.figures: £21m annual depreciation vs £6m annual budget; £618m needed to eliminate backlog; normalised spend £3,051/km
findings.quote: From the evidence provided we understand that funding is around 60% of what is required for steady-state maintenance, and that current levels of Government funding are insufficient to prevent long term deterioration of roads and bridges.

findings.headline: Adult social care unplanned care home price pressure rising to £33.3m by 2029/30, dependent on untested Choice Policy delivering savings
findings.detail: Care home fees for older adults are rising beyond planned annual uplifts due to turnover and new placement costs exceeding closure costs. This unplanned pressure was £3.4m in 2025/26 and is forecast to grow to £33.3m by 2029/30. The council is consulting on a Choice Policy intended to mitigate this, but full delivery is flagged as a big risk in the MTFS. Implementation pace must be monitored.
findings.matters: This is the single largest uncontrolled cost pressure in the forecast. If the Choice Policy fails or takes longer than planned, the council faces a widening deficit. Care market dynamics are outside the council's direct control.
findings.figures: £3.4M in 2025/26 rising to £33.3M by 2029/30; £8.9M immediate cost pressure in year
findings.quote: This is placing an additional cost pressure on the MTFS, estimated at £3.4M in 2025/26 and rising to £33.3M by 2029/30 unless mitigated through planned policy and funding decisions.

findings.headline: DSG accumulated deficit forecast to reach £200m by March 2028, when statutory override ends and council must absorb it
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit stood at £53.6m in March 2025 and is forecast to rise to £90m by March 2026. When the statutory override expires in April 2028, the projected deficit is £200m. The council will need to borrow significantly to cover this, but national funding arrangements remain unconfirmed.
findings.matters: A £200m hole when the statutory protection ends is a material covenant risk. It forces borrowing or reserve depletion at a defined date with no agreed government funding solution.
findings.figures: £53.6m deficit at March 2025; circa £90m by March 2026; £200m forecast at March 2028
findings.quote: The Statutory Override for the DSG Deficit is set to end in April 2028 meaning SCC reserves could be required to demonstrate ability to fund the deficit. At March 2025, the deficit stands at £53.6m. This is forecast to increase to circa £90m by March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Half Yearly Treasury Management Report for the Period Ended 30 September 2025
findings.headline: £15m LOBO loan repaid after lender exercised call option at 7.29% interest rate; two remaining LOBO loans (£18m) face call dates in December 2025 and January 2026
findings.detail: Staffordshire repaid a £15 million LOBO loan in early 2025/26 when the lender exercised a call option and increased the interest rate from 4.275% to 7.29%, forcing the council to use cash reserves rather than accept the higher rate. The council retains two LOBO loans totalling £18m: Dexia £10m at 4.140% with call date 11 December 2025, and FMS £8m at 4.500% with call date 30 January 2026. The report explicitly states 'it is anticipated that the lenders may exercise their call options during the latter half of 2025/26', indicating these forced refinancing events will occur within weeks.
findings.matters: LOBO call options create forced refinancing events outside the council's control; the 7.29% rate demanded by the first lender (vs 4.275% original) demonstrates material rate shock is possible, and similar moves would force either higher debt costs or further cash depletion.
findings.figures: £15m repaid at 7.29% (increased from 4.275%); £18m remaining LOBO debt: Dexia £10m at 4.140% (call date 11/12/2025), FMS £8m at 4.500% (call date 30/01/2026)
findings.quote: During the first six months of the year the County Council repaid a £15 million LOBO loan early due to the lender exercising their call options and increasing the interest rate payable on the loan from 4.275% to 7.29%.

findings.headline: Waste disposal tonnage 8% over budget
findings.detail: Total waste tonnage handled in Q1 2025/26 reached 57,135 tonnes against a target of <52,726. Red-rated, indicating operational overspend on waste management.
findings.matters: Waste disposal is a fixed-cost service; overages represent unbudgeted operational expenditure and may indicate inefficiency or increased demand.
findings.figures: 57,135 tonnes vs <52,726 target
findings.quote: Overall waste tonnage <52,726 57,135 (Q1 25/26) Red

findings.headline: Education, Health and Care Plans issued in time for only 29% of applications
findings.detail: Only 29% of EHCPs are issued within the statutory 20-week timescale, against a 49.1% target. Red-rated with a declining trend, indicating worsening performance.
findings.matters: EHCP delays impact school funding formulas and delay resource allocation for children with special needs; persistent delays suggest capacity constraints in the SENCO function.
findings.figures: 29% vs >49.1% target
findings.quote: % of EHCPs issued in time (20 weeks) >49.1% 29% (Jul 25) Red

findings.headline: 12 looked-after and SEND-eligible children not transitioned to adult services by age 18
findings.detail: The council has 12 cases where children known to social care as eligible for adult services were not referred by the statutory transition age, against a zero target. This represents complete failure of the transition duty.
findings.matters: Failures to transition young people into adult services represent governance breakdowns with potential safeguarding and financial consequences, as continuity of care is interrupted.
findings.figures: 12 cases vs 0 target
findings.quote: Looked after children & children with SEND likely to be eligible for care & support as adults, known to children's social care before 17th b'day & referred to adult social care after 17th b'day 0 12 (Jul 25) Red

findings.headline: Child protection conferences not held on time
findings.detail: Only 93.3% of initial child protection conferences are held within statutory timescales, against a 100% requirement. Red-rated, with no improvement trend.
findings.matters: Failure to convene child protection conferences on time is a breach of statutory safeguarding duty and indicates capacity constraints in the safeguarding team.
findings.figures: 93.3% vs =100% target
findings.quote: % of initial child protection conferences held in time =100% 93.3% (Jul 25) Red

findings.headline: Children's social work assessments 6 percentage points below statutory requirement
findings.detail: Only 79.1% of children's social work assessments are completed on time, against an 85% target. The metric is red-rated with a static trend, indicating persistent capacity or process constraints.
findings.matters: Consistent failure to meet statutory assessment timescales indicates the children's social care service may be under-resourced and at risk of further compliance failures.
findings.figures: 79.1% vs >85% target
findings.quote: % Childrens social work assessments completed on time >85% 79.1% (Jul 25) Red

findings.headline: Adoption timescales 26% longer than target
findings.detail: Children awaiting adoption are taking 536 days on average to move into adoptive families, significantly exceeding the 426-day target. This extends the duration for which the council must fund expensive foster or residential placements.
findings.matters: Delayed adoptions prolong the council's liability for expensive out-of-home care, extending costs by months per child.
findings.figures: 536 days vs <426 target
findings.quote: Average number of days between a child entering care and moving in with its adoptive family, adjusted for foster carer adoptions. <426 536 (Q1 25/26) Red

findings.headline: Children in care rate 16% above target
findings.detail: The rate of children in care stands at 75.5 per 10,000 population, significantly above the <64.7 target. This indicates elevated demand for costly foster and residential placements. The metric is red-rated and unchanged from previous months.
findings.matters: Each additional child in care generates ongoing costs for foster placements, residential care, and case management. A 16% overage represents substantial unplanned expenditure.
findings.figures: 75.5 per 10,000 vs <64.7 target
findings.quote: Rate (number) of children in care per 10,000 <64.7 75.5 (Jul 25) Red

findings.headline: Rising placement and care costs in Children's Services and Adult Care Commissioning are driving reserve depletion
findings.detail: The council identifies key pressures in these two highest-cost services due to rising placement and care costs. While an overall Q2 underspend of £1.274m is reported, these specific demand pressures are being absorbed through targeted use of reserves and interventions, not operational efficiency. This signals structural budget challenges that cannot be solved by baseline savings.
findings.matters: Lenders evaluate councils on whether they can absorb cost shocks within baseline operations. Rising demand in the two most expensive services, being offset by reserves rather than efficiency, indicates future years may face structural deficits, service cuts, or borrowing needs if these pressures continue.
findings.figures: Overall underspend £1.274m (0.17% of balanced budget); specific figures for Children's Services and Care Commissioning pressures in Appendices 4-5
findings.quote: Key pressures remain in Children's Services and Care Commissioning due to rising placement and care costs, though these are largely offset by reserves and targeted interventions.

findings.headline: Staffordshire must restructure from two-tier to unitary authority and submit its proposal to government by 28 November 2025.
findings.detail: Central government has mandated replacement of all two-tier local authorities with unitaries by end of parliament. Staffordshire received statutory invitation on 5 February 2025. Cabinet has selected an East-West option (Staffordshire West and Staffordshire East, including Stoke-on-Trent) over the previous single-county unitary proposal. The detailed business case will be approved by Cabinet on 4 November 2025 before government submission.
findings.matters: Major restructuring affects the council's financial structure, borrowing profile and operational viability during transition; lenders need to understand the chosen model's financial and operational implications.
findings.figures: Submission deadline 28 November 2025; Cabinet decision 4 November 2025; eight reorganization options analyzed
findings.quote: This statutory invitation asked for councils in the area to submit proposals for how Staffordshire's local government will be reorganised to one or more unitary authorities. This proposal must be submitted to government by 28 November 2025.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation option published despite Cabinet opposition
findings.detail: Although Cabinet does not support Local Government Reorganisation, the council has published an options analysis in September 2025 as required by government. The proposed East-West model is framed as providing 'best balance of financial sustainability, service quality, and local needs' and includes Stoke-on-Trent to address its financial challenges.
findings.matters: Reorganisation creates uncertainty for lenders around authority stability, service continuity, and financial integration. The specific inclusion of Stoke-on-Trent (which has known financial difficulties) signals the council may be planning or expecting a merged structure with greater financial risk.
findings.figures: East-West model proposed in September 2025 to include Stoke-on-Trent
findings.quote: The proposed East-West model provides the best balance of financial sustainability, service quality, and local needs. It also meets the government's requirement to include Stoke-on-Trent and address its financial challenges.

findings.headline: Workforce recruitment paused from 15 September with sickness levels above target
findings.detail: The council has implemented a workforce efficiency review with a recruitment pause from 15 September. Sickness absence is at 11.6 days per employee (rolling 12 months) against an 11-day target. While the council notes month-on-month improvement and attributes progress to the 'Safe and Well' scheme, sickness remains elevated.
findings.matters: A recruitment freeze during a period of rising demand (children in care up, EHCP backlog growing, assessments behind) suggests either financial constraint or a mismatch between demand and headcount planning.
findings.figures: 11.6 days sickness absence vs 11-day target
findings.quote: Workforce Efficiency review has commenced with a recruitment pause in place from 15th September. Although sickness levels remain above target (11.6 days compared to a target of 11), they show further month-on-month improvement in levels of long-term sickness, suggesting that the 'Safe and Well' scheme is having a positive impact.

findings.headline: Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards backlog: 427 requests outstanding after 21 days vs 400 target
findings.detail: Outstanding Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards requests are 427 against a target of 400, exceeding the target by 27. These are assessments required before restricting the freedom of people lacking capacity, often in social care settings. The council notes it is prioritising requests on receipt to manage risk.
findings.matters: A backlog in safeguarding assessments is a compliance and risk issue. These measures protect vulnerable adults; backlogs can force councils to make placement decisions without proper legal authority.
findings.figures: 427 requests outstanding vs 400 target
findings.quote: The number of requests outstanding after 21 days remains above target (427 against a target of 400).

findings.headline: Children's social work assessments below target: 79.1% vs 85% despite additional resourcing
findings.detail: Timeliness of social work assessments is at 79.1%, below the 85% target and national average. The council has agreed additional resourcing, with 4 peripatetic social workers in place from mid September. Performance has improved from 74.7% last year, but the need for emergency staffing suggests ongoing capacity stress.
findings.matters: Assessment delays put children at risk and often force reactive crisis spending. The fact that improvement required emergency contract staff indicates the permanent structure is undersized.
findings.figures: 79.1% vs 85% target; improvement from 74.7% year-on-year
findings.quote: Performance has improved since the same period last year (74.7% to 79.1%) but remains below the national average and target of 85%. Additional resourcing agreed, with 4 peripatetic social workers in place from mid September to help address capacity concerns.

findings.headline: Capital programme slipped £10.8m, schools and highways affected
findings.detail: The latest capital forecast is £159.8m, down £10.8m from Q1's £170.6m forecast. Slippage is driven by the Schools and Highways programmes plus strategic reviews of projects in Countryside and Libraries. No explanation given for the timing or whether this represents delayed spend or cancelled schemes.
findings.matters: Capital slippage can signal either poor planning, external blockers, or reduced investment capacity. Schools and highways are usually frontloaded; delay here suggests possible wider constraint.
findings.figures: £159.8m latest forecast vs £170.6m Q1 forecast (-£10.8m)
findings.quote: The latest capital forecast is £159.8m, compared to the Quarter 1 forecast of £170.6m, a decrease of £10.8m due to slippage in the Schools' and Highways' programmes plus the projects in Countryside and Libraries are currently under review.

findings.headline: EHCP timeliness collapsed: only 29% issued within 20 weeks against 49.1% target
findings.detail: The timely issuance of Education, Health and Care Plans has fallen to 29% over the last 12 months (down from 30% the previous month). The council has 480 initial assessments in progress that have already exceeded the statutory 20-week deadline, which will continue to impact performance once issued. Council expects stabilisation only from Feb 2026.
findings.matters: EHCP delays generate legal liability, parental challenge, and often force spend on interim provision or private placements. A backlog of 480 overdue cases suggests systemic capacity or process failure.
findings.figures: 29% on-time vs 49.1% target; 480 initial assessments exceeding deadline
findings.quote: The overall timeliness rate over the last 12 months continues to fall (29% from 30% last month) as more overdue plans are finalised. This remains lower than the target of 49.1% (national average). There are currently 480 initial assessments in progress that have exceeded the deadline which will continue to impact the overall rate once issued in coming months.

findings.headline: Looked after children 16% above benchmark, rising year-on-year
findings.detail: Rate of children in care at 75.5 per 10,000 (1,306 children), compared to statistical neighbour average of 64.7. This is an increase of 19 children from the same point last year (1,287). This is one of the largest cost drivers in children's services.
findings.matters: Looked-after children placements are high-cost. A rate 16% above neighbours indicates either higher need, commissioning risk, or both, and a rising trend suggests the pressure is worsening.
findings.figures: 75.5 per 10,000 vs 64.7 statistical neighbour average; 1,306 children vs 1,287 last year (+19)
findings.quote: The rate of children in our care at the end of July was 75.5 compared to the statistical neighbour average of 64.7 (this relates to 1,306 children, an increase of 19 children compared to the same point last year where we had 1,287 children in our care).

findings.headline: Savings plan severely behind: only £0.315m delivered of £6.678m target
findings.detail: As at Q2, the council has delivered just £0.315m of the £6.678m savings target. The latest forecast shows £1.274m (0.17%) saving by year-end, with pressures in Adults' and Children's social care being offset only by use of reserves. This means the council is drawing down reserves rather than achieving the planned efficiency savings.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can deliver its efficiency savings plans. Drawing reserves to cover unfunded pressures rather than controlling costs is a warning sign.
findings.figures: £0.315m delivered; £6.678m target; £1.274m (0.17%) forecast saving by end of 2025/26
findings.quote: There are £0.315m savings that are delivered as at Quarter 2. The latest revenue forecast shows a saving of £1.274m (0.17%) by the end of 2025/26 with pressures arising in Adults' and Children's social care being offset by use of reserves

findings.headline: Children's Services is forecasting a £0.500m overspend
findings.detail: The quarterly forecast shows Children's Services with a revised budget of £163.189m but forecast outturn of £163.689m. This overspend is being offset by a corresponding £0.500m saving in Wellbeing & Partnerships within the same portfolio, resulting in no net variation for Children and Families.
findings.matters: Children's services are a structural pressure area for councils, often indicating rising demand or cost pressures. An overspend signals the council is managing tighter-than-budgeted costs in this sensitive area.
findings.figures: £0.500m overspend; Revised budget £163.189m; Forecast outturn £163.689m
findings.quote: Children's Services 163.189 163.689 0.500

findings.headline: Revenue outturn forecast missed its accuracy target, varying more than 2% from budget
findings.detail: The council's revenue outturn forecast fell outside the acceptable +/-2% variance range against the overall revenue budget, triggering an amber (not met by small margin) rating. The other indicators — debtor recovery, supplier payment timeliness, and MTFS savings tracking — all met or exceeded their targets.
findings.matters: A forecast that misses its variance target suggests either emerging service pressures the council did not anticipate or control weaknesses in understanding its own spend. Lenders and finance directors need to know whether the council can predict its outturn.
findings.figures: Amber indicator; debtors at £30.638m (under £32.915m limit); supplier payments 98% within 30 days (vs 90% target)
findings.quote: The council's most recent revenue outturn forecast did not vary by more than +/-2% when compared to the overall revenue budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - 2025-26 Internal Audit Plan - Progress Update
findings.headline: Staffing turnover and previous recruitment failures in the internal audit function
findings.detail: The audit service experienced three unsuccessful recruitment exercises during 2024/25, unforeseen staffing sickness absences, and continues to rely on external audit contracts and agency staff to meet delivery targets. This staffing instability has already delayed delivery of the 2024/25 audit plan and impacted the start of 2025/26.
findings.matters: High turnover and difficulty recruiting in the audit/control function may indicate broader HR retention issues across the council, or that the role/environment is unattractive, both of which affect financial governance quality.
findings.figures: Three unsuccessful recruitment exercises in 2024/25; staffing sickness absences causing delays; two new senior auditors started 1 September 2025; one recruitment still pending mid-November 2025; reliance on external contracts and agency staff
findings.quote: During 2024/25 and the first two quarters of 2025/26, the Internal Audit Service has operated with a number of vacant posts (following three unsuccessful recruitment exercises during 2024/25) as well as suffered unforeseen staffing sickness absences which led to delays in the delivery of the 2024/25 Internal Audit Plan.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - 2025-26 Internal Audit Plan - Progress Update
findings.headline: Multiple control failures identified: duplicate payments, unauthorised spending, and fraud recoveries
findings.detail: Continuous controls monitoring identified eight duplicate invoice payments totalling £8,389, three instances of staff meeting expenditure contrary to Financial Regulations under investigation, and recovered £1,550 from inappropriate cash withdrawals and £3,942 from a deceased person with active care provisions. These findings indicate control environment weaknesses across payments and cash handling systems.
findings.matters: Recurring control failures in payments, expense approval, and benefit administration suggest systemic weaknesses that could mask larger losses or expose the council to continuing fraud and error.
findings.figures: £8,389 duplicate invoice payments; £1,550 recovered from cash withdrawal misuse; £3,942 recovered from deceased person in payment system; three procedural breaches under investigation
findings.quote: Eight Duplicate invoice payments totalling £8,389. These findings are in the process of being verified and the recovery of duplicate payments will be monitored. At the time of writing, there are three instances of expenditure for staff meetings which are believed to be contrary to the Council's Financial Regulations.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - 2025-26 Internal Audit Plan - Progress Update
findings.headline: Five audits cancelled and audit coverage reduced due to staffing constraints
findings.detail: The council has cancelled five planned system audits to rebalance the audit plan following three unsuccessful recruitment exercises in 2024/25, staffing sickness, and vacant posts. The cancelled audits include Corporate Asset Management Strategy, Long Service Awards, Economic Growth Programme, Green Solutions, and Care Market Management & Development. Only one vacant post remains despite recruitment of three senior auditors.
findings.matters: A weakened internal audit function reduces the council's ability to identify and manage financial control risks, which increases regulatory and financial risk for lenders.
findings.figures: Five audits cancelled; one vacant post remaining; three unsuccessful recruitment exercises; only 29% of planned audit work commenced by 15 September 2025
findings.quote: To bring the 2025/26 Internal Audit Plan back into balance and having considered the additional work conducted as well as staff recruitment and retention issues, five system audit reviews have been cancelled so far this year.

news_drafts.headline: Authorized borrowing of £580m but forecast only £330m—43% gap
news_drafts.lead: Large gaps between authorized and forecast borrowing raise questions about whether capital plans are at risk or whether assumptions have shifted. A lender would need to understand why actual deployment falls so far short of authorization.

news_drafts.headline: Long-term investment forecast cut 88% from budget: £245m to £30m
news_drafts.lead: A dramatic cut in planned investment signifies either tighter liquidity or deferred capital schemes. Either would concern a lender assessing the council's cash flow and capital programme delivery.

news_drafts.headline: LOBO loans with uncertain call dates create refinancing risk the council cannot quantify with standard limits
news_drafts.lead: LOBO calls create refinancing risk that is not fully predictable; if called, the council must refinance at prevailing market rates regardless of the interest rate environment.
